Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas · Civic life: news, government & the law

integrate verb

become, or make someone, part of a group or a whole

also integration, be integrated, fit in, merge, become one

classical

Sall. C. 6.2 (Lewis & Short)
Liv. 2.48.1: ut cum Patribus coalēscerent animī plēbis (Lewis & Short)

coalēscō, coalēscere, coaluī, coalitum

verb, third conjugation, intransitive; with cum and the ablative, or in with the accusative

grow together; of peoples and groups, become one, integrate

Literally of things that grow together: a graft with its tree, a wound that closes (Varro, Pliny). Of peoples, the word of Sallust, Livy and Tacitus; never in Cicero (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • 1asciscō: vowel before sc unmarked (Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked). The present stem’s i (as in sciscō) is not marked by Lewis & Short or by de Vaan (s.v. sciō), and Bennett was not to hand; the perfect ascīvī, ascītum is long. Left unmarked until checked.

    asciscō1, asciscere, ascīvī, ascītum — take in, admit (as citizen, ally, member)

    verb, third conjugation, transitive · also used · classical · Cic. Arch. 2 fin.: putētis asciscendum fuisse (Lewis & Short); Caes. B.G. 3.9.10: sociōs sibi … adsciscunt (Lewis & Short)

    Of the group that takes someone in: as a citizen, an ally, a son-in-law, a king. Also, of laws and opinions, to adopt, approve. Also spelled adsciscō.

Examples

  • ut cum Patribus coalēscerent animī plēbis

    so that the feelings of the commons might merge with those of the senatorsLiv. 2.48.1 (Lewis & Short)

  • perficiam ut hunc A. Licinium nōn modo nōn sēgregandum, cum sit cīvis, ā numerō cīvium, vērum etiam, sī nōn esset, putētis asciscendum fuisse

    I shall make you think that Archias should not only not be cut off from the citizens, being one, but should have been admitted even if he were notCic. Arch. 2 fin. (Lewis & Short)

  • Novī vīcīnī facile nōbīscum coaluērunt.

    The new neighbours have fitted in with us easily.composed

See also join, include, society.

SourcesLewis & Short: coalesco · Lewis & Short: ascisco

Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), s.v. sciō.

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.

The example sentences marked “composed” are ours.
